extracted.intended_audience: general educated readers interested in aesthetics, taste, and literary essays (readers of The Spectator)
extracted.subtask_description: A sequence of early-18th-century Spectator essays by Joseph Addison discussing the pleasures of the imagination (primarily those arising from sight), the sources of those pleasures, and their application to art, landscape, and architecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sight as primary source of imaginative pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Our Sight is the most perfect and most delightful of all our Senses. It furnishes the Imagination with its Ideas; we cannot have a single image in the fancy that did not make its first entrance through the Sight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sight supplies the largest variety of ideas, allows remote observation and long continued action without fatigue, and is a more delicate, diffusive kind of touch. Use visible objects (actual view, paintings, statues, descriptions) as the principal means to excite the imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: pleasures of the imagination (primary and secondary)
rubrics_metrics.description: By the Pleasures of the Imagination are meant such as arise from visible Objects, either when we have them actually in our View (primary), or when we call up their Ideas in our Minds by Paintings, Statues, Descriptions, or memory (secondary).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between pleasures arising from present sights and those from recalled or invented images; treat both as legitimate but different sources of enjoyment and aesthetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary pleasures arise from Greatness, Uncommonness, or Beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Those Pleasures of the Imagination which arise from the actual View and Survey of outward Objects proceed from the Sight of what is Great, Uncommon, or Beautiful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing or evaluating scenes (natural or artistic), consider whether the object displays magnitude (vast views), novelty/strangeness, or intrinsic beauty — any of these will strongly affect the imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greatness (bulk/extent) produces pleasurable astonishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Greatness refers not only to the bulk of a single object but to the largeness of a whole view — e.g., open champaign country, vast deserts, mountains, wide expanses of water — which give a pleasing astonishment and sense of liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designs that provide spacious horizons or unconfined panoramas increase imaginative pleasure; avoid overly confined or cramped visual compositions that imply restraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty and uncommonness stimulate curiosity and pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Everything that is new or uncommon raises a Pleasure in the Imagination because it fills the Soul with an agreeable Surprise, gratifies Curiosity, and varies human life from repeated shows of the same things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce variation, unexpected elements, or movement (e.g., waterfalls, shifting scenes) to renew attention; be wary of monotony which quickly tires the eye.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty gives immediate inward satisfaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty immediately diffuses a secret Satisfaction and Complacency through the Imagination, and the first discovery strikes the Mind with an inward Joy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beauty may be species-specific (what is beautiful in our own kind) or manifest in form, colour, proportion, and arrangement. Evaluate or create elements for their immediate affective impact rather than only intellectual justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Species-specific beauty (sexual/biological basis)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a kind of Beauty that appears in our proper species which works most warmly — e.g., creatures are attracted by the colours or tints of their own kind; such beauty promotes generation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that certain aesthetic responses are deep-seated and biologically rooted; in representational art or description, fidelity to species-typical cues can evoke strong imaginative pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary kinds of beauty: colour, symmetry, proportion, arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: A second kind of Beauty in products of Art and Nature arises from gaiety or variety of colours, symmetry and proportion of parts, arrangement and disposition of bodies, or a just mixture and concurrence of all together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging crafted works (painting, architecture, gardens), assess colour harmony, proportion, compositional arrangement, and balanced variety as sources of delight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colour is especially powerful for the imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: The Eye takes most Delight in Colours; poets borrow epithets from colours more than any other topic — e.g., glorious shows at rising and setting of the Sun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use vivid, well-chosen colour and light effects (sunrise/sunset, cloud staining) to address the imagination directly; colour relationships can set tone and emotional response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination of senses heightens imaginative pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: The assistance of another sense (sound — music of birds, fall of water; smell — fragrances) heightens the pleasures of the Imagination and makes colours and verdure appear more agreeable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In composition or experience design, combine visual elements with sound and scent to produce a synergistic effect; multimodal stimuli strengthen imaginative engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion and change increase interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Scenes that perpetually shift or contain motion (rivers, waterfalls, ships in progress) entertain the sight every moment with something new and prevent fatigue from fixed, settled objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In representational art, landscaping, or narrative description, incorporate movement or dynamic elements to sustain attention and refresh the imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety prevents satiety of the eye
rubrics_metrics.description: Variety, by calling the mind every instant to something new, relieves satiety and improves what is great or beautiful; fixed sameness tends to tire the spectator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor varied composition — changing textures, colours, and forms — over monotony; ensure pacing and varied focal points in longer visual experiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Works of nature generally surpass works of art in grandeur
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature often displays more vastness and immensity than art; the rough, careless strokes of Nature can be more bold and masterly than the nice touches of Art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating artificial landscapes or art, aim to evoke or resemble the grand, unconfined qualities of nature rather than purely decorative neatness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resemblance of art to nature yields double pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: When products of Art resemble those of Nature, pleasure arises both from their agreeableness to the eye and from their similitude to other objects, giving a double principle of delight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In architecture, painting, or gardening, borrow natural forms and effects to gain the compensatory pleasures of both artifice and perceived naturalness; many successful designs imitate natural irregularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artificial works improve when they imitate natural irregularity
rubrics_metrics.description: Artificial works are more pleasing when they present a kind of 'artificial rudeness' resembling natural forms (English vs French/Italian gardens; Chinese preference for concealed art).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overly geometric, 'mathematical' pruning or symmetry that exposes artifice; favor designs that conceal the rule and suggest a natural genius in arrangement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architecture and garden design: greatness both in bulk and manner
rubrics_metrics.description: Greatness in architecture may relate to the bulk/body of the structure or to the manner in which it is built; ancient structures show superior magnitude, but manner (design and effect) also matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess buildings by both their scale and by how their construction and disposition affect the imagination — consider proportion, vista, and how the structure contributes to spacious prospects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imaginative pleasures are healthful and restorative
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasures of the Fancy are more conducive to Health than those of the Understanding; delightful scenes disperse grief and melancholy and set the animal spirits in pleasing motion (Sir Francis Bacon cited).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value and recommend visual and imaginative entertainments (poems, prospects, paintings) for psychological and physical refreshment; they require less strenuous thought while promoting well-being.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polite imagination: cultivated receptivity to visual art
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'Man of a Polite Imagination' can converse with a picture, find an agreeable companion in a statue, and meet with secret refreshment in a description; this sensibility expands one's sphere of innocent pleasures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate familiarity with visual arts and descriptions to gain subtle pleasures; education and habituation increase one's capacity to enjoy and derive property from visual objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final/teleological causes for aesthetic pleasures (philosophical justification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some final causes: delight in greatness encourages contemplation of the divine; delight in novelty encourages pursuit of knowledge; delight in beauty encourages propagation of species — these explain why such pleasures are annexed to certain ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these teleological accounts as higher-order justification for rewarding certain design choices (greatness, novelty, beauty) — they function as explanatory principles rather than practical rules.
